title: System Design & Scalability
requirement: Architect, design, implement high-performance, scalable, secure full-stack apps.

questions.question: Walk me through how you approach designing a new system from scratch.
questions.answer: I start with the numbers: users, reads and writes per second, data size, latency targets. Then the data model and API, since they're hardest to change. I go boring first, load balancer, stateless services, database, and add caches, queues or shards only where numbers demand.
questions.keyTakeaway: Numbers first, data model second, boring architecture third, complexity only where proven.

questions.question: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?
questions.answer: Vertical scaling is a bigger machine. It's simple but capped, and still a single point of failure. Horizontal adds machines, so it's elastic, but it needs stateless services and a shared-data plan. I scale up until it hurts, then out.
questions.keyTakeaway: Up is simple but capped; out is elastic but demands statelessness and shared-state design.

questions.question: What role does a load balancer play, and what must services do to sit behind one?
questions.answer: It spreads traffic by health and pulls failed instances out, so services must be stateless and expose honest health endpoints. Tuning matters: checks too eager let a GC pause cascade into lost capacity, too lazy send users to dead pods.
questions.keyTakeaway: The balancer routes around failure; services owe it statelessness and honest health checks.

questions.question: Where do caches fit in a scalable system, and what do you cache first?
questions.answer: I cache at the edge (browser, CDN), in-process, and in shared stores like Redis, starting with expensive, frequently read data. Every entry gets a TTL as a safety net, explicit invalidation where correctness matters, and request coalescing against stampedes.
questions.keyTakeaway: Cache hot, expensive reads; TTL for safety, invalidation for freshness, coalescing for stampedes.

questions.question: Explain the CAP trade-off and how it shows up in practical decisions.
questions.answer: During a partition a store has to pick consistency or availability. Partitions will happen, so I decide per data type. Payments and inventory lean consistent, because unavailable beats wrong. Carts and feeds lean available. I also name the reconciliation job that cleans up after the stale window, which is what separates this from reciting the theorem.
questions.keyTakeaway: Choose C or A per data type under partition, and design the reconciliation path.

questions.question: How do you design a system to survive infrastructure failure?
questions.answer: I remove single points of failure with multiple zones and automated failover, then add timeouts, backoff retries, circuit breakers and graceful degradation. And I rehearse failover, because untested failover is a hypothesis.
questions.keyTakeaway: Redundant everything, degrade gracefully, and rehearse failover before you need it.

questions.question: The application got slow at peak load. How do you find the bottleneck?
questions.answer: I trace requests and watch latency percentiles and saturation per tier, CPU, memory, pools, queue depths, until the time concentrates somewhere. Usual suspects are a missing index or exhausted connections. I separate waiting from computing, then re-test at the same load.
questions.keyTakeaway: Trace the request, read saturation signals, separate waiting from working, then re-test at peak.

questions.question: How do you do back-of-the-envelope capacity estimation for a new feature?
questions.answer: I start from daily active users, actions per user and the read-to-write ratio, then spread that over peak hours to get per-second rates. I size storage from record size and growth, and check what I want to cache fits in memory. Then I test each tier against realistic per-node capacity to find the first wall. The numbers are coarse, but they show which architectures are plausible.
questions.keyTakeaway: Users to per-second rates to per-tier capacity: find the first wall before designing around it.

questions.question: How does consistent hashing distribute data across servers, and why is hash modulo N a problem?
questions.answer: With hash(key) % N, adding one server remaps most keys and floods the cache with misses. Consistent hashing puts servers and keys on a ring, a key belongs to the first server clockwise, and a change moves only the neighboring arc. Virtual nodes flatten the skew. Cassandra uses it.
questions.keyTakeaway: Ring placement plus virtual nodes: membership changes move only neighboring keys.

diagram.title: Hash modulo N versus consistent hashing

questions.question: Describe how an architecture evolves from a single server to millions of users.
questions.answer: I start with one box, then split the database out so tiers scale and fail independently. Next a load balancer with a stateless web tier, then database replication: primary for writes, replicas for reads. After that a cache and CDN for hot reads, and a queue for slow or spiky work. Each step answers a measured pain, and multi-region comes last.
questions.keyTakeaway: Grow by measured pain: split tiers, balance stateless web, replicate, cache and CDN, queue the spikes.

questions.question: Why do retry policies need exponential backoff, and why is jitter essential?
questions.answer: Immediate retries hammer a struggling dependency and deepen the outage. Exponential backoff spaces them out, say 100 ms, 200, 400, with a cap. Jitter matters because clients that failed together would otherwise retry together and recreate the spike. I add timeouts and a circuit breaker too.
questions.keyTakeaway: Exponential backoff spaces retries, but only jitter keeps a million clients from retrying as one spike.

code.snippet:
retry:
  maxAttempts: 5
  initialBackoffMs: 100
  multiplier: 2.0
  maxBackoffMs: 10000
  jitter: full

questions.question: When would you put a message queue between a service and its workload?
questions.answer: I use a queue when demand spikes and the work needs no immediate answer, like email or media processing. The service enqueues and acknowledges instantly, so a ten-x burst buffers instead of exhausting pools. I size workers for sustained load and watch depth, since a silent backlog is a delayed outage. Queues level load, they don't create capacity.
questions.keyTakeaway: A queue buffers spikes so workers run at sustained capacity, but it levels load and never creates it.

questions.question: How do you choose between object, block, and file storage for a workload?
questions.answer: By access pattern. Block is a raw disk on one machine, low latency, so databases live there. File, like NFS, suits shared trees. Object is a flat, effectively infinite, cheap HTTP namespace, which fits backups, media and data lakes.
questions.keyTakeaway: Pick storage by access pattern: block for databases, file for shared trees, object for write-once petabytes.

questions.question: Why does offset pagination fall apart at scale, and what replaces it?
questions.answer: Offset pagination scans and discards every earlier row, so deep pages get slow. Keyset uses a cursor, where created_at and id are less than the last row, backed by an index, so each page is a constant-cost seek. The trade-off is no page 37 jump, and the sort key must be unique.
questions.keyTakeaway: Keyset cursors turn every page into an indexed seek, so page depth never changes the cost.

questions.question: How do graceful degradation and failover differ, and when do you build each?
questions.answer: Failover swaps a broken component for a healthy replica, which fits when the component is the system, like the primary database. Degradation keeps a reduced feature alive, like static recommendations, through explicit per-feature switches decided in advance. Failover costs idle standby, degradation costs experience, and users mind a slow page less than an error.
questions.keyTakeaway: Failover replaces the broken replica, degradation ships a reduced feature, and both need prebuilt switches.

questions.question: What are SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets, and how do they change design decisions?
questions.answer: An SLI is the measured signal, an SLO the target, say 99.9 percent of requests under 300 ms, and the error budget is the allowed failure, about 43 bad minutes a month. When it's empty, feature work pauses for stability. I set targets per service, not five nines everywhere.
questions.keyTakeaway: SLOs convert reliability into a spendable error budget that gates feature work when exhausted.

questions.question: How does write-ahead logging make a database crash-safe?
questions.answer: The database appends each change to a log on stable storage before touching data pages, so a commit is one sequential write. After a crash, recovery replays the log, redoing committed changes and undoing uncommitted ones. I watch WAL latency, since a full or slow log stops every write.
questions.keyTakeaway: Log the change before applying it: commit becomes one sequential fsync and crashes replay the log.

questions.question: What is a thundering herd, and how do you stop one at a popular cache key?
questions.answer: A thundering herd is when a hot cache entry expires and hundreds of concurrent requests hit the origin with the same expensive query. Coalescing fixes it: the first miss takes a lock and fetches, the rest wait for that result. I also use jittered TTLs and stale-while-revalidate.
questions.keyTakeaway: Park concurrent misses behind one lock so the herd collapses into a single origin fetch.

questions.question: Walk me through the actual arithmetic you'd do to size QPS for a new feature.
questions.answer: Say fifty million daily users at twenty views each, so a billion views a day. Divide by 86,400 for about twelve thousand QPS average, maybe twenty-four thousand at peak. A 95 percent cache hit rate drops origin reads to just over a thousand QPS. The first number to exceed node capacity is the bottleneck.
questions.keyTakeaway: Divide daily volume by 86,400, double for peak hour, then let cache hit rate rewrite the origin number.

questions.question: How do you handle a hot key that overwhelms one shard of your cache or database?
questions.answer: A hot key sends everything to one shard, so that node saturates while others idle and adding nodes doesn't help. I spot it with per-key metrics. For reads I replicate the value, for writes I salt the key and aggregate on read, and I keep a process-local copy in front.
questions.keyTakeaway: Hot keys defeat horizontal scaling, so replicate, salt, or locally pin the few keys everyone wants.

questions.question: When would you fan out feed writes to followers instead of fanning in reads?
questions.answer: Fan-out on write pushes each post into every follower's precomputed timeline, so reads are cheap. In practice I hybridize: push for normal users, but pull a celebrity's posts at read time and merge. Pushing to a hundred million inboxes would be a self-inflicted denial of service.
questions.keyTakeaway: Push writes to follower feeds for cheap reads, but pull celebrity posts at read time and merge.

questions.question: How do you budget latency when a system spans multiple regions?
questions.answer: US East to West is around sixty to seventy ms round trip, Europe to Asia over two hundred. I budget a request as a sum of hops and keep reads local with replicas per region and asynchronous cross-region writes. A globally consistent write routes to one leader or pays for consensus, so few operations should.
questions.keyTakeaway: Inter-region physics is fixed, so serve reads locally and reserve cross-region consensus for the few writes that need it.

questions.question: How do you systematically hunt for single points of failure in a running system?
questions.answer: I draw the real dependency graph, including DNS, certificates, brokers, feature flags and IAM, then kill each node on paper and ask what stops. The sneaky ones are rarely the web tier. Think a shared Kafka cluster, one NAT gateway, or the config service. I separate control plane from data plane failures, since serving during an orchestrator outage is survivable. For each real SPOF I fix it, spread it, or record the accepted risk with its blast radius.
questions.keyTakeaway: Hunt SPOFs by killing every node on paper, control plane included, then fix, spread, or accept with eyes open.

questions.question: How does the rate at which data changes decide whether caching it is worth it?
questions.answer: Caching pays when data is read many times between changes, so I compute churn first, change frequency over read frequency. A live bid that changes on every read has such a short hit window that the cache serves stale data and adds invalidation work. Staleness tolerance sets the TTL, and for high churn I use short TTLs or skip the cache.
questions.keyTakeaway: Compute churn first, changes per read, because it sets both the TTL and whether caching pays at all.

no.label: High churn
no.note: short TTL, or skip the cache

questions.question: How do you keep joins affordable once related data lives on different shards?
questions.answer: The cheapest distributed join never crosses the network. I pick the shard key so rows queried together land together, like a tenant's data on one shard. Otherwise I denormalize and accept the cost of keeping copies consistent. Scatter-gather is for analytics, never the request path.
questions.keyTakeaway: Co-locate rows by shard key or denormalize, because a join across the network is the expensive kind.

questions.question: What is the difference between global and local load balancing, and why do you need both?
questions.answer: Local balancing spreads traffic across instances in a region and routes around dead ones. Global balancing picks the region per user via DNS, anycast or a traffic manager using health and latency, and absorbs region failures. It's coarse since DNS caches for minutes, so I add a capacity floor per region.
questions.keyTakeaway: Global balancing picks the region with coarse, slow signals; local balancing fixes instances fast, and both are required.

rows.label: Local: pick an instance
rows.note: L4 or L7, fast health checks

questions.question: Explain bulkheads and cell-based architecture, and what each contains.
questions.answer: A bulkhead gives each downstream its own connection pool and thread budget, so a hung recommendations service exhausts only its own. Cells apply that to the whole stack: independent app and data store per slice of tenants behind a thin router, so a bad deploy kills one cell. They duplicate operations, so I'd adopt them after shared fate has bitten.
questions.keyTakeaway: Bulkheads wall off per-dependency resources, cells wall off whole tenant slices, and both cap blast radius.

questions.question: Why does idempotency become non-negotiable once you add retries and queues?
questions.answer: Retries and redelivery mean the same operation runs twice by design, causing double charges or duplicate shipments. The fix is an idempotency key: a client-generated id stored with the outcome, so a repeat returns the stored result, with a TTL and a unique constraint. Exactly-once delivery doesn't exist, but exactly-once effects do, by deduplicating on a stable key.
questions.keyTakeaway: Retries and redelivery are certain, so dedupe on idempotency keys for exactly-once effects, not delivery.
